problems.description: Wholesale replacement of the seeded Flask/sqlite baseline (138 lines removed, -1 file refactored) rather than incremental extension — acceptable for a greenfield session, but discards the seed's deliberate seams (models/routes/error handling) that later sessions were meant to build on.
test_app.py has 2 convention violations (PascalCase where snake_case is expected; module-level constants not UPPER_CASE), per the 0.82 convention score.

broadcast() uses asyncio.gather with no return_exceptions=True and no try/except around sends — a single failed send (dropped/closed connection) can raise and abort delivery to all remaining healthy clients.
Threading RLock inside a single-threaded asyncio server is unnecessary; the event loop already serializes access, so the lock adds concurrency complexity without benefit.
JSON parse errors are echoed back to clients with the raw exception string, leaking internal error details.

strengths: Clean two-class decomposition (ClientRegistry, NotificationServer) with single responsibilities and strong typing throughout.
Centralized message construction with type validation, ISO-8601 timestamps, and payload type checks.
Per-message error isolation: malformed frames produce a system error reply instead of dropping the connection.
Health endpoint reporting live connected-client count via process_request.
Measured improvement over baseline: bugs 0, smells -1, duplications 0.0%, convention score 0.82.
commit_reviews.summary: Strong greenfield architecture for an async WebSocket notification server with clean class decomposition, validated message handling, and per-message error isolation — though it fully replaces rather than extends the seeded Flask baseline, and test_app.py carries two convention violations.

problems.description: test_app.py: 'Classes should use PascalCase' flagged, but the AST diff shows +0 classes added, so this appears to be a pre-existing or analyzer artifact rather than new code.
test_app.py: 'Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' flagged by SonarQube; the added get_json helper is a snake_case function, so this also looks like analyzer noise or a pre-existing issue.
Cognitive complexity +23 and +2 smells in the connection handler from the new subscribe/unsubscribe branches and channel validation; readable but worth extracting a dispatch helper.

strengths: Channel subscription model layered cleanly onto ClientRegistry with the same RLock discipline and type hints as existing code
Disconnect cleanup correctly purges stale channel subscriptions and prunes empty channels
Backwards-compatible signatures: broadcast/build_message treat channel as optional, so existing clients and the /health endpoint are unaffected
Input validation rejects non-string or empty channel names with a system error message
New /channels and /channels/{name}/subscribers endpoints covered by a raw-HTTP test helper
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, backwards-compatible channel feature with good registry hygiene, validation, and tests; the only friction is minor analyzer convention flags in the test file (discrepant with the +0 classes AST measurement) and slightly increased handler complexity.

problems.description: MessageStore performs blocking synchronous SQLite I/O (save/list) directly on the asyncio event loop, which can stall all WebSocket connections under load; should run in a thread executor or use an async driver.

RedisBroker is constructed unconditionally in NotificationServer.__init__, so a missing optional `redis` package or unreachable localhost Redis breaks server startup even for single-node use that never needs the broker.
SonarQube cognitive complexity +30 is concentrated in deliver() and broker lifecycle code (nested branches, isawaitable dispatch), making the integration logic harder to reason about.
MessageStore.close() and RedisBroker.close() are defined but never wired into a shutdown/teardown path, leaking SQLite handles and Redis sockets across restarts.
Channel name extraction via string slicing key[len(prefix):-len(":clients")] is fragile and recomputed per key inside scan_iter; hoist the prefix length and parse once.
Static analysis flags test_app.py for 2 convention violations: test classes not PascalCase and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: persistence (MessageStore), transport/subscription state (RedisBroker), and orchestration (NotificationServer) split into focused classes
Production-aware Redis usage: pipelines for atomic multi-key operations and scan_iter instead of blocking KEYS
Dependency-injection friendly constructor (redis_client/redis_url/database_url with env fallbacks) aids testability
Graceful optional-dependency import guard for the redis package
app.py code itself respects conventions: PascalCase classes, snake_case methods, UPPER_CASE constants, full type hints
commit_reviews.summary: Session 3 integration cleanly adds SQLite persistence and Redis pub/sub with strong separation of concerns and testable seams, but unconditional broker construction, blocking SQLite on the event loop, and +30 cognitive complexity introduce technical debt.

problems.description: test_app.py: Classes should use PascalCase (measured SonarQube violation, unchanged by this commit's app.py work)
test_app.py: Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE (measured SonarQube violation)
ClientRegistry type hints downgraded from ServerConnection to Any (25+ lines), weakening static typing across the module contrary to the codebase's typed-signature convention

WebSocketTransport.on_connect/on_disconnect are empty no-ops while handle_connection simultaneously accepts on_connect/on_message/on_disconnect callbacks — duplicated lifecycle ownership with an ambiguous contract

BaseTransport abstract signatures use Any instead of a Protocol, so the seam leaks; WebSocket-specific serve()/handle_connection live only on the concrete class, meaning the abstraction is not fully transport-agnostic

strengths: Extracts a clean injectable transport seam (BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport), isolating WebSocket concerns from the notification server
Measured improvement: smells -1 and cognitive complexity -1 with no new bugs or duplications (+0 bugs, +0.0% dup)
Additive refactor that preserves the existing ClientRegistry/MessageStore/RedisBroker structure and async lifecycle; no new dependencies
Env-driven factory (_create_transport) with explicit validation and a WebSocket default, keeping backward compatibility
commit_reviews.summary: A solid incremental refactor that lowers complexity and adds a transport extension point, offset by a module-wide downgrade to Any typing and a partially duplicated lifecycle contract.

problems.description: Rate limiting is placed on RedisBroker (check_rate_limit), a pub/sub transport class. It works only because RedisBroker is mandatory and owns the Redis handle, but it couples a cross-cutting concern to the broker rather than a dedicated limiter (the app_match.py variant used a separate RateLimiter class).

_cleanup_expired_messages runs a synchronous SQLite DELETE on the event loop in a while True loop with a hardcoded 3600s interval; the delete is not offloaded via asyncio.to_thread and the interval is not configurable.
test_rate_limit_returns_error_without_dropping_connection asserts error == {... 'timestamp': error['timestamp']}, a self-referential tautology that cannot fail on the timestamp field.

from urllib.parse import parse_qs, urlsplit is duplicated inline inside the /messages and /history handlers instead of being a top-level import (mirrors the existing /messages pattern, so consistent, but smelly).
SonarQube reports +1 smell and +27 cognitive complexity from this commit, concentrated in the growing monolith _on_message and process_request handlers.

strengths: Features land in the correct architectural homes: persistence in MessageStore (history/delete_older_than), config + lifecycle in NotificationServer, Redis state in RedisBroker.
Background cleanup task lifecycle mirrors the existing _listener_task pattern (created in start, cancelled/awaited in close).
Parameterized SQL queries with RLock guards and atomic 'with self._lock, self._connection' transactions, consistent with existing MessageStore style.
Pagination via limit+1 has_more technique; results ordered timestamp ASC, id ASC per the story spec.
Robust input handling: _positive_int_env validation and timezone-aware 'since' parsing that rejects naive timestamps.
Tests added in the established fixture/get_json style covering rate limiting, history ordering, and pagination.
commit_reviews.summary: Strong, spec-complete implementation of the cross-cutting session (rate limiting, history endpoint, TTL cleanup) that fits the existing architecture and patterns well, with only minor cohesion and test-assertion weaknesses; note that the two reported convention violations (test_app.py PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE constants) are positive-pattern misses in a file this commit added no classes or constants to, not violations introduced here.

compounding_issues: S1's single NotificationServer class owning WebSocket + HTTP + client registry made the file grow to 442 lines by S5; the S4 transport refactor extracted only the WebSocket listener, leaving HTTP, SQLite, Redis, and rate limiting in the monolith
The S4 BaseTransport abstraction is structural only — _create_transport raises for any non-websocket TRANSPORT value, so the pluggable-transport promise is never exercised
S1's threading.RLock over asyncio-managed client dicts persisted every session, mixing threading and asyncio primitives in an event-loop-only codebase
S3's Redis integration degrades silently on any ping failure (no logging or surfaced status), which can mask deployment misconfigurations at runtime
The Flask seed app.py was almost entirely discarded in Session 1's greenfield rewrite, wasting the seed scaffolding
key_decisions: S1 discarded the seed in favor of a clean monolithic async server owning both WebSocket and HTTP in one class
S2 extended the wire protocol with channel subscribe/unsubscribe and kept a channel registry in sync across subscribe, disconnect, and cleanup paths
S3 added Redis pub/sub fan-out plus SQLite message persistence with graceful single-instance degradation when Redis is absent
S4 extracted a BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport abstraction so the server routes messages through a pluggable transport layer
S5 added per-client rate limiting (Redis-backed with local fallback), a message TTL retention policy with a background cleanup loop, and a /history HTTP endpoint
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across all five sessions. The arc moves logically from a greenfield monolithic core (S1) through a protocol-level feature (channels, S2) and integration (Redis pub/sub + SQLite persistence, S3), to an architectural refactor extracting a transport abstraction (S4), and finally cross-cutting operational concerns (rate limiting, retention TTL, history endpoint, S5). Tests grew in lockstep with implementation (4 to 10 tests; server grew 154 to 442 lines), and the final commit passes 15 tests with 1 skip. Each session built cumulatively on prior protocol and storage decisions rather than reworking them, though the S4 refactor was partial and did not prevent continued monolith growth.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session arc that progressed naturally from greenfield core to channels, Redis/SQLite integration, a transport abstraction, and finally cross-cutting operational concerns, with quality and test coverage improving monotonically throughout.
